The approval of a provincial development scheme costing Rs 2,500 million, with 40% financed by a foreign loan, requires the sanction of the Departmental Development Working Party (DDWP) [1]. The DDWP has the authority to approve projects up to Rs 2,000 million provided foreign aid/foreign exchange is less than 25% of the total cost. Since this project has 40% foreign financing, it exceeds the DDWP's approval limit, and thus, the DDWP is barred from approving it. The scheme would instead require approval from the Provincial Development Working Party (PDWP) or a higher authority, as the DDWP's delegated powers do not extend to projects with foreign financing exceeding 25% [1].

The Departmental Development Sub-committee (DDSC) is barred from approving such a scheme because it is only empowered to recommend and approve schemes up to Rs 100 million relating to the provincial ADP [2]. The DDSC does not have the authority to approve projects of this magnitude, especially those involving significant foreign financing, which requires higher-level scrutiny and approval.

The full approval path for a provincial development scheme of Rs 6,000 million with no foreign aid begins with the Departmental Development Working Party (DDWP) at the provincial level. According to [1], the DDWP, chaired by the Administrative Secretary concerned, has the authority to approve schemes up to Rs 400 million. However, for schemes exceeding this amount, the approval process involves the Provincial Development Working Party (PDWP) [2]. The PDWP, as the highest body at the provincial level, is responsible for approving development projects and can consider schemes even below its powers if referred by the DSC or DDWP [2]. 

For a scheme of Rs 6,000 million, the PDWP would be the approving forum at the provincial level. The PDWP ensures that the scheme aligns with the objectives of the national, provincial, or sectoral plans [2]. Once approved by the PDWP, the scheme is submitted to the Planning Commission for further processing and approval [2]. The Planning Commission communicates the approval through an authorisation letter, which is followed by administrative approval and sanction for incurring expenditure [3]. The administrative approval is issued by the concerned provincial department [3].

No federal forum is involved in the approval process for a provincial scheme with no foreign aid, as the DDWP and PDWP operate at the provincial level [1]. The federal Development Working Party (DDWP) is only involved if the scheme involves foreign aid or exceeds the provincial approval limits [4].

Technical approval refers to the formal approval granted to development project proposals that are compliant with the standards and procedures set by the Planning Commission. This approval is based on the findings and recommendations of independent quality assurance reports, cost & benefit analysis, and risk assessment, where required [1]. The technical approval process is a prerequisite for further stages of project approval and implementation.

Anticipatory approval, on the other hand, is a special type of approval granted before the full preparation of the project proposal, typically for projects that require immediate action due to urgent needs or donor financing. Anticipatory approval is granted only to the Chairman ECNEC and is valid for a specific period, after which the case must be processed afresh [2]. It is considered an "extraordinary jurisdiction" and cannot be re-delegated to maintain financial discipline and control [2]. Anticipatory approval is required for projects above a certain cost threshold and must be accompanied by detailed reasons and justification [3].

The standard procedure for approving development projects in Pakistan involves several stages and is governed by specific laws and rules. Initially, project proposals undergo a technical approval process, where they must comply with the standards and procedures set by the Planning Commission [1]. Once technical approval is granted, the project is submitted for approval by the relevant development working parties, such as the Provincial Development Working Party (PDWP) or the Departmental Development Working Party (DDWP), depending on the project's scale and jurisdiction [2][3]. For projects costing up to Rs. 200 million, the Departmental Development Sub-committee (DDSC) is authorized to approve them [4]. 60 million, the DDWP is responsible [3]. 2,000 million, the Departmental Development Working Party (DDWP) has sanctioning powers, provided foreign aid/foreign exchange is less than 25% of the total cost [5]. 

Once approved, the project is followed by administrative approval, which is issued by the concerned federal ministry for federally-sponsored projects or the provincial department concerned for provincial projects. This administrative approval includes the total cost, foreign exchange component, and any other riders imposed by the approving body, and it is distinct from the sanction for incurring expenditure on the scheme, which is issued on a yearly basis [6]. The activation of the project is achieved through the appointment of a Project Director, with specific guidelines for the appointment of an Independent Project Director based on the project's cost [7][8][9]. For projects costing Rs. 1000.00 million and above, the appointment of an Independent Project Director is mandatory [7]. For projects costing below Rs. 3,000 million, such cases should be submitted for approval of the CDWP by providing proper justification [8]. The Project Director should not be transferred during the currency of the project [7][8].
